title: Molecular Surveillance and Genomic Characterization of Influenza A(H3N2) Viruses From a Secondary‐Care Surveillance Site in Pakistan During the 2025–2026 Winter Season

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory viral infections, particularly Influenza A and SARS‐CoV‐2, remain major public health concerns in endemic settings such as Pakistan, where high influenza‐like illness burden and limited genomic data underscore the need for surveillance to guide vaccine strategies.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study assessed respiratory virus circulation and genetic diversity among ILI cases at a secondary‐care hospital in Islamabad during the 2025–2026 winter season.
analysis.methods: Among 170 qRT‐PCR‐tested cases, Influenza A was detected in 24.1%, SARS‐CoV‐2 in 1.17%, and Influenza B was not detected. Whole‐genome sequencing of 21 Influenza A(H3N2) isolates revealed co‐circulation of subclade K (52.4%), J.2.2 (28.6%), and J.2 (9.5%).
analysis.main_results: Influenza A positivity was slightly higher in females (25.0%), with highest burden in individuals aged 11–20 years. Phylogenetic analysis showed subclade K clustering with recent isolates from North America, Oceania, Europe, and WHO‐recommended 2026–2027 Northern Hemisphere H3N2 vaccine strains, whereas J.2 and J.2.2 aligned with earlier vaccine‐like strains. NA analysis showed predominance of clade B.4.2.2 associated with K‐lineage and relatedness to recent North American strains. Subclade K exhibited conserved HA substitutions (K2N, S144N, N158D, I160K, Q173R, T328A) and HA2 S49N with limited variation. No antiviral resistance mutations were detected.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Overall, findings demonstrate predominance and genetic stability of H3N2 subclade K and support continuous genomic surveillance for vaccine strain selection and influenza preparedness.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform vaccine strain selection by showing subclade K's alignment with WHO‐recommended strains and highlight the importance of genomic surveillance in influenza preparedness.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was conducted at a single secondary‐care hospital, limiting generalizability. However, the evidence strength is high due to comprehensive genomic analysis and direct detection methods.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted molecular surveillance of Influenza A(H3N2) viruses in Pakistan during the 2025–2026 winter season. Among 170 ILI cases, 24.1% tested positive for Influenza A, with no Influenza B detected. Whole-genome sequencing of 21 H3N2 isolates revealed co-circulation of subclade K (52.4%), J.2.2 (28.6%), and J.2 (9.5%). Subclade K clustered with recent global isolates and WHO-recommended vaccine strains, showing conserved HA substitutions and no antiviral resistance. The findings highlight the predominance of genetically stable subclade K and emphasize the need for continuous genomic surveillance to guide vaccine strategies and influenza preparedness.

title: Evolution of swine influenza surveillance and one health governance in Taiwan: from zoonotic risk management to integrated preparedness.

analysis.scope_and_question: This review examines the evolution of swine influenza surveillance and One Health governance in Taiwan, focusing on the pathogen influenza A viruses (IAVs), the host swine populations, and the population context of Taiwan with 5.5 million pigs and 23.4 million people. The central question is how swine influenza surveillance has evolved from fragmented monitoring to a coordinated One Health framework to address zoonotic risks and pandemic preparedness.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This is a review article that describes the development of veterinary surveillance strategies in Taiwan, including the transition from fragmented, event-driven monitoring to a coordinated One Health governance framework. The review incorporates routine whole-genome sequencing, targeted serological surveillance, and coordinated data exchange across sectors, as well as the use of AI-enabled technologies for pandemic preparedness.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The key conclusion is that strengthened veterinary surveillance under a One Health framework can improve the detection of viral reassortment events, enhance traceability of viral spread, and support timely risk assessment in intensive livestock systems. The Taiwanese experience demonstrates that integrating molecular epidemiology, veterinary field monitoring, and cross-sector communication provides practical value for pandemic preparedness.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review identifies gaps in notification capacity exposed by A(H1N1)pdm09 and human H1N2v infections. While the surveillance systems have been established to link animal, human, and environmental health, the review does not specify any remaining controversies or unresolved mechanisms, focusing instead on the evolution and benefits of the integrated approach.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The implications highlight the practical value of integrating molecular epidemiology, veterinary field monitoring, AI-enabled technologies, and cross-sector communication under a One Health framework. The Taiwanese experience offers a replicable pathway for other countries to overcome swine influenza surveillance fragmentation and strengthen pandemic preparedness, emphasizing the importance of coordinated surveillance across human and animal health sectors.

analysis.summary_en: This review examines the evolution of swine influenza surveillance and One Health governance in Taiwan, tracing its development from fragmented monitoring to a coordinated framework. The review highlights Taiwan's experience with 5.5 million pigs and 23.4 million people as a case study for addressing zoonotic risks through strengthened veterinary surveillance. Key milestones include mass vaccination, pandemic responses, and zoonotic detections of H1N2v, demonstrating bidirectional viral exchange. The integration of whole-genome sequencing, serological surveillance, and AI technologies under One Health has improved detection of reassortment events and viral traceability. The findings offer a practical, replicable model for other countries to enhance pandemic preparedness by overcoming surveillance fragmentation and fostering cross-sector coordination.

title: A systematic meta-analytic comparative evaluation of seasonal influenza vaccine effectiveness from test-negative design studies in the Northern Hemisphere pre/post COVID-19 pandemic

analysis.scope_and_question: This review evaluates seasonal influenza vaccine effectiveness (VE) against A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), influenza B, and B/Victoria in the Northern Hemisphere, comparing pre- (2010/11-2019/20) and post- (2022/23-2024/25) COVID-19 pandemic periods across three age groups (6 months-17 years, 18-64 years, ≥65 years).
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A systematic meta-analysis of 85 published test-negative design (TND) studies was conducted. Pooled VE estimates were calculated using inverse-variance random-effects meta-analysis, with heterogeneity quantified by I2 and statistical differences tested by χ2.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Post-pandemic VE against A(H3N2) and influenza B was significantly higher in 6-month-17-year-olds and 18-64-year-olds compared to pre-pandemic. Conversely, VE against A(H1N1)pdm09 was lower post-pandemic in 18-64-year-olds. No significant differences were observed for ≥65-year-olds, and B/Victoria data were limited.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The authors note that factors other than population immunity may explain the observed VE changes. Data for B/Victoria were limited, and no significant differences were found in the ≥65-year-old group, leaving gaps in understanding age-specific VE dynamics.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Further research is needed to explore factors beyond population immunity influencing post-pandemic VE, particularly in older adults and for B/Victoria. Surveillance should continue to monitor VE trends across age groups and virus subtypes.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic meta-analysis compared seasonal influenza vaccine effectiveness (VE) before and after the COVID-19 pandemic using 85 test-negative design studies. Post-pandemic VE against A(H3N2) and influenza B was significantly higher in children and adults, while VE against A(H1N1)pdm09 decreased in adults. No significant changes were observed in older adults, and B/Victoria data were limited. The authors suggest factors beyond population immunity may explain these findings, highlighting the need for further research on VE determinants and continued surveillance across age groups and subtypes.

title: Epistasis facilitates the long-term antigenic evolution of the influenza B virus hemagglutinin

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand how epistasis facilitates the long-term antigenic evolution of the influenza B virus hemagglutinin, addressing the need to balance antigenic drift with purifying selection pressure to maintain functionality.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study characterized the influenza B virus hemagglutinin over 8 decades of circulation in humans, focusing on genetic and antigenic changes.
analysis.methods: The research involved characterizing genetic and antigenic changes in the influenza B virus hemagglutinin over time, identifying mutations and deletions at specific positions and their epistatic interactions.
analysis.main_results: The study found continuous genetic diversification in influenza B virus hemagglutinin, with antigenic changes driven by recurring mutations and deletions at positions 136, 150, 162-165, 197, and 203, forming complex epistatic networks.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that epistatic networks modulate antigenic impact and generate permissive backbones for immune escape with limited fitness cost, highlighting similarities and differences with A(H3N2) evolution.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings support the development of genotype-to-phenotype prediction tools for influenza viruses, emphasizing the need to capture epistatic outcomes for accurate predictions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate, as the study's focus on influenza B virus may limit generalisability to other influenza strains, and the reliance on historical data introduces potential biases.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the long-term antigenic evolution of the influenza B virus hemagglutinin, revealing that epistatic networks facilitate antigenic changes while maintaining viral fitness. By analyzing 8 decades of data, the researchers identified recurring mutations and deletions at specific positions that form complex interactions, enabling immune escape with minimal fitness cost. The findings highlight similarities and differences with A(H3N2) evolution and support the development of genotype-to-phenotype prediction tools, though the focus on influenza B virus may limit broader applicability. The study underscores the importance of epistasis in balancing antigenic novelty with viral functionality.

title: Effectiveness of seasonal influenza vaccine against dominant A(H1N1)pdm09 in adults ≥ 60 years: a multicenter test-negative design in Zhejiang, China, 2024–2025

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of seasonal influenza vaccine against the dominant A(H1N1)pdm09 virus in adults aged ≥ 60 years during the 2024–2025 influenza season in Zhejiang, China, as data on real-world vaccine effectiveness in this population were still lacking.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A multicenter, retrospective test-negative design (TND) was adopted in this study, which enrolled all or a systematic sample of patients aged ≥ 60 years presenting with influenza-like illness (ILI) at designated sentinel hospitals in six cities of Zhejiang Province from October 2024 to July 2025.
analysis.methods: Epidemiological data were collected, respiratory specimens were obtained, and laboratory assays were conducted to detect influenza virus types and subtypes, with adjustments made for age, sex, chronic comorbidities, calendar week, and city.
analysis.main_results: Of the 4694 enrolled elderly patients with ILI, 1587 (33.81%) were influenza-positive, with A(H1N1)pdm09 being the dominant subtype (93.3%). Vaccination coverage was 32.72% (1536/4694).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study provides evidence-grounded interpretation of the effectiveness of the seasonal influenza vaccine against A(H1N1)pdm09 in the elderly population, highlighting the moderate protection observed and the waning effectiveness over time.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform public health strategies for influenza vaccination in the elderly population, particularly regarding the timing and frequency of vaccination to maintain effectiveness against A(H1N1)pdm09.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for confounding factors, but the evidence is strong as it is based on a large sample size and adjusted for key demographic and health variables.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the effectiveness of the seasonal influenza vaccine against the dominant A(H1N1)pdm09 virus in adults aged ≥ 60 years in Zhejiang, China, during the 2024–2025 influenza season. Using a multicenter, retrospective test-negative design, the researchers enrolled patients with influenza-like illness (ILI) and collected epidemiological data and respiratory specimens. They found that 33.81% of enrolled patients were influenza-positive, with A(H1N1)pdm09 being the most prevalent subtype. The overall vaccine effectiveness (VE) was 53.3% (95% CI: 45.4–60.2), with varying effectiveness across age groups. VE decreased over time, from 58.0% within 59 days post-vaccination to 42.8% between 60 and 180 days. The study highlights the moderate protection provided by the vaccine against A(H1N1)pdm09 in the elderly, suggesting that consecutive vaccination may help maintain effectiveness. These findings have implications for public health strategies, particularly in optimizing vaccination schedules for this vulnerable population.

title: Identifying the viral and epidemiological factors behind the apparent global extinction of influenza B/Yamagata

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate which epidemiological and immunological factors were primarily responsible for the apparent global extinction of the influenza B/Yamagata lineage after the COVID-19 pandemic.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The researchers developed a global transmission model for the two influenza B lineages (B/Yamagata and B/Victoria) and simulated the impacts of pandemic-related contact reductions to explain their divergent outcomes.
analysis.methods: The study used mechanistic transmission modeling combined with worldwide influenza surveillance data, implementing a transient reduction in contacts to mimic pandemic effects and identify parameter values that recapitulated pre-pandemic coexistence and post-pandemic outcomes.
analysis.main_results: The results indicate that B/Yamagata's extinction was mainly driven by its lower basic reproduction number, making it particularly vulnerable during the early phase of the pandemic, while B/Victoria narrowly avoided extinction during the same period.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that differences in cross-immunity and immune escape are insufficient to explain the observed outcome, and the novelty lies in demonstrating that Yamagata's lower intrinsic transmissibility was the primary factor in its extinction.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings inform influenza eradication efforts and biosafety policy, including assessing the feasibility of B/Victoria eradication through vaccination and the potential for B/Yamagata's re-emergence if reintroduced.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate, as the study relies on model simulations and surveillance data, which may not capture all real-world complexities, though the model successfully recapitulated observed outcomes.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the apparent global extinction of influenza B/Yamagata after the COVID-19 pandemic. The researchers developed a global transmission model for the two influenza B lineages and simulated pandemic-related contact reductions. Their findings indicate that B/Yamagata's lower basic reproduction number made it particularly vulnerable during the pandemic's early phase, while B/Victoria narrowly avoided extinction. The study concludes that differences in cross-immunity and immune escape were insufficient to explain the outcome, with lower intrinsic transmissibility being the primary factor. These results inform influenza eradication efforts and biosafety policy, including the feasibility of B/Victoria eradication and the potential for B/Yamagata's re-emergence if reintroduced.

title: Epidemiological characteristics analysis of childhood influenza A virus infections in Hebei, China (2020–2024)

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to analyze the epidemiological and infection characteristics of childhood influenza A virus infections in Hebei, China, from 2020 to 2024, to provide a basis for influenza prevention and control among children.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective analysis was conducted on epidemiological and clinical data of children with influenza A virus infection who were hospitalized in Hebei Province from January 2020 to December 2024.
analysis.methods: Clinical specimens were analyzed using nucleic acid extraction reagents with automatic extraction on the Smart LabAssist-32 nucleic acid extractor. A 13-pathogen multiplex PCR detection kit combined with the GeXP multiplex gene expression analysis system was used for testing.
analysis.main_results: A total of 298,810 specimens from children with upper and lower respiratory tract infections were collected. Among these, 60,928 specimens were positive for influenza A virus (detection rate: 20.39%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that pediatric influenza A virus infections in Hebei Province exhibit a clustered age distribution, pronounced seasonal variation, and a high co-infection rate.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform targeted surveillance and protective measures for children aged 1–5 years and during the winter season, which is critical for optimizing influenza prevention and control strategies, clinical diagnosis, and treatment.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for selection bias, but the evidence is strong with a high confidence level due to the large sample size and statistical significance of the results.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed the epidemiological characteristics of childhood influenza A virus infections in Hebei, China, from 2020 to 2024. It found that the detection rate of influenza A virus was 20.39% among 298,810 specimens collected from hospitalized children. The infection rate peaked in winter at 29.04% and was lowest in spring and summer at 5.4%. The study also reported a 26.34% co-infection rate with pathogens such as rhinovirus, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. These findings highlight the seasonal variation and high co-infection rate of influenza A virus in children, suggesting the need for enhanced surveillance and protective measures during winter and for children aged 1–5 years. The study's retrospective design and potential for selection bias are limitations, but the large sample size and statistically significant results support a high confidence assessment.

title: Flu Mutation Explorer: an Interactive Platform for Mapping Host Adaptation Mutations in Influenza A Viruses

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the challenge of interpreting the biological significance of viral mutations in influenza A viruses, particularly amino acid replacements associated with host adaptation, in the context of rapid expansion of genome sequencing data.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study presents the Flu Mutation Explorer, an interactive web application that combines large-scale influenza phylogenies with a manually curated database of reported mammalian adaptation mutations.
analysis.methods: The underlying database comprises over 1.5 million publicly available IAV sequences and over 1000 mutations associated with mammalian adaptation, enabling users to query protein sequences, visualise amino acid distributions across viral lineages, and examine host-specific conservation patterns.
analysis.main_results: The Flu Mutation Explorer enables users to identify adaptation mutations with links to supporting literature and includes case studies demonstrating its use in assessing amino acid conservation at sites of interest and in rapidly identifying candidate mammalian adaptation mutations during the ongoing H5N1 panzootic.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: By integrating genomic, phylogenetic, and functional information into an intuitive interface, the Flu Mutation Explorer lowers the barriers to interpreting influenza sequences for specialists and non-specialists alike.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The platform facilitates the exploration and interpretation of IAV genetic variation, supporting surveillance efforts and aiding in the rapid identification of candidate mammalian adaptation mutations during influenza outbreaks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is high as the study presents a well-developed interactive platform with a comprehensive database and demonstrates its utility through case studies, though the evidence is from a preprint and not yet peer-reviewed.

analysis.summary_en: The Flu Mutation Explorer is an interactive web application designed to address the challenges of interpreting influenza A virus mutations, particularly those associated with host adaptation. It integrates large-scale phylogenies with a curated database of over 1.5 million IAV sequences and 1000+ mammalian adaptation mutations. The platform enables users to query protein sequences, visualize amino acid distributions, examine host-specific conservation patterns, and identify adaptation mutations with supporting literature. Case studies demonstrate its utility in assessing amino acid conservation and rapidly identifying candidate mutations during the H5N1 panzootic. By combining genomic, phylogenetic, and functional data in an intuitive interface, the tool lowers barriers for both specialists and non-specialists in influenza sequence interpretation.

title: Risk Factors for Mortality Associated With Influenza Infection in Patients With Hematologic Malignancies: A Cross‐Sectional Descriptive Observational Study

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate influenza infection in patients with hematologic malignancies and identify the risk factors associated with mortality. Cancer patients, especially those with hematologic malignancies, are considered among the most vulnerable groups at risk for severe outcomes from influenza infection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This cross-sectional descriptive observational study included 90 patients with confirmed influenza infection and hematologic malignancies. The data collected included demographic information, cancer type and status, influenza type, symptoms, laboratory and radiologic findings, length of hospital stay, ICU admissions, and mortality rate.
analysis.methods: Methods involved collecting data on demographic information, cancer type and status, influenza type, symptoms, laboratory and radiologic findings, length of hospital stay, ICU admissions, and mortality rate from 90 patients with confirmed influenza infection and hematologic malignancies.
analysis.main_results: The mean age of patients was 34.3 ± 26.7 years (median 34, range 2–91). Nearly half (49.3%) were in the maintenance phase of treatment, and 80% were infected with influenza A. ICU admission was significantly linked to older age (p = 0.002), comorbidity (p = 0.003), lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) (p = 0.02), muscle ache (p = 0.03), and malignancies including MM, CML, and AML (p = 0.02). Higher mortality was observed in patients with MM or AML (p = 0.01), comorbidities (p = 0.02), and LRTIs (p = 0.04).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study identified ICU admission as significantly associated with older age, the presence of at least one comorbidity, LRTI, and body muscle aches. Age-adjusted analysis confirmed MM, LRTIs, and comorbidities as potential strong predictors of mortality in this cohort.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform surveillance and risk assessment strategies for influenza in hematologic malignancy patients, highlighting the importance of monitoring for comorbidities, LRTIs, and specific malignancies such as MM and AML.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its observational design and the need for validation in larger studies. The age-adjusted analysis identified MM, LRTIs, and comorbidities as potential strong predictors of mortality, but the evidence strength is moderate due to the study's design and sample size.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional observational study investigated influenza infection in patients with hematologic malignancies to identify risk factors for mortality. The study included 90 patients with confirmed influenza infection and HMs, collecting data on demographics, cancer type, influenza type, symptoms, and clinical outcomes. Results showed that ICU admission was significantly linked to older age, comorbidities, lower respiratory tract infections, and certain malignancies like MM, CML, and AML. Higher mortality was observed in patients with MM, AML, comorbidities, and LRTIs. The study concluded that MM, LRTIs, and comorbidities are strong predictors of mortality in this population. While the findings are relevant for understanding influenza outcomes in cancer patients, the study's observational design and small sample size limit the strength of the evidence, necessitating further research.

title: LncRNA ckATP1A1-AS1 inhibits influenza A virus replication by mediating innate immune responses and suppressing viral nuclear import

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza A viruses pose an ongoing threat to humans and other species because of their zoonotic potential, and the functions and mechanisms of action of most IAV-associated lncRNAs remain unclear.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study identified ckATP1A1-AS1 as an antiviral host lncRNA induced by IAV infection and performed functional analyses to determine its effects on viral replication.
analysis.methods: Functional analyses demonstrated that ckATP1A1-AS1 overexpression restricted infection by multiple IAV subtypes, whereas ckATP1A1-AS1 knockdown enhanced viral replication, and mechanistic studies revealed its interaction with viral nucleoprotein and regulation of interferon responses.
analysis.main_results: ckATP1A1-AS1 overexpression restricted infection by multiple IAV subtypes, whereas ckATP1A1-AS1 knockdown enhanced viral replication, and it suppresses viral ribonucleoprotein assembly and reduces viral polymerase activity.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: This study identifies the novel chicken antisense lncRNA ckATP1A1-AS1 as a key antiviral factor with a unique dual mechanism: it is transcriptionally activated by transcription factor JUN and upregulates interferon-β and key interferon-stimulated genes to positively regulate the type I interferon immune response.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings establish ckATP1A1-AS1 as a key antiviral lncRNA that restricts IAV replication by coordinating innate immune signaling and directly targeting several steps in the viral replication cycle, which may inform future therapeutic strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study provides strong mechanistic evidence for the antiviral role of ckATP1A1-AS1 in IAV infection, but the evidence is based on in vitro experiments and may not fully represent in vivo conditions.

analysis.summary_en: This study identifies the novel chicken antisense lncRNA ckATP1A1-AS1 as a key antiviral factor that inhibits influenza A virus replication. The research demonstrates that ckATP1A1-AS1 is induced by IAV infection and functions through a dual mechanism: it is transcriptionally activated by the transcription factor JUN, which enhances the expression of interferon-β and key interferon-stimulated genes, thereby boosting the type I interferon immune response. Additionally, ckATP1A1-AS1 directly interacts with the viral nucleoprotein, disrupting its binding to importin α5, impairing its oligomerization, and blocking the nuclear import of viral ribonucleoprotein complexes. This leads to suppressed viral ribonucleoprotein assembly and reduced viral polymerase activity. Functional analyses confirmed that overexpression of ckATP1A1-AS1 restricts infection by multiple IAV subtypes, while its knockdown enhances viral replication. These findings provide strong mechanistic evidence for a novel host defense mechanism against influenza A viruses.

title: A chicken interferon stimulated gene screen reveals limited genes restricting influenza replication

title: From neuraminidase inhibitors to novel mechanisms: expanding therapeutic strategies against influenza

analysis.scope_and_question: Seasonal influenza viruses (A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), B/Victoria, and historical B/Yamagata) cause approximately one billion infections and up to 650,000 respiratory deaths annually. The central question is how to expand therapeutic strategies beyond current limitations.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This review critically evaluates the antiviral landscape, focusing on next-generation cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitors (CENIs), resistance implications across all approved drug classes, translational barriers in host-directed therapies and biologics, and H5N1 pandemic preparedness.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Scaffold-level optimization (e.g., Suraxavir marboxil, ZX-7101A, onradivir) can reduce resistance emergence rates. However, all approved classes share a failure pattern: single-target dependence, low-fitness-cost resistance mutations, and a therapeutic window most patients do not reach. Combination therapy shows promise for resistance prevention, but virological benefit does not consistently translate to clinical outcomes in hospitalized patients.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Host-directed therapies and biologics face translational obstacles: their biological window of activity precedes clinical presentation, and systemic biologics cannot achieve inhibitory concentrations at the respiratory mucosal surface. For H5N1, preparedness relies on a single observationally supported drug class; baloxavir is absent from most stockpiles, and no randomized trial data exists for any antiviral in human H5N1 infection.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Adaptive trial infrastructure, diversified stockpiling to include next-generation CENIs, and equitable global antiviral access are the most urgent priorities in influenza therapeutics.

analysis.summary_en: This review evaluates therapeutic strategies against seasonal influenza, highlighting limitations of current antivirals, including time-dependent efficacy, low resistance barriers, and evidence gaps in high-risk populations. It examines next-generation CENIs, resistance patterns, and translational challenges for host-directed therapies. Key findings include scaffold-level optimization reducing resistance emergence and combination therapy's promise without consistent clinical benefit. Urgent priorities include adaptive trials, diversified stockpiling, and global access to next-generation antivirals, with critical gaps in H5N1 preparedness.

title: SNHG15 Positively Regulates Influenza Virus Infection Through Its Association With miR-153 and RABL2A.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza viruses cause seasonal epidemics, and current vaccines do not fully protect against them. This study focuses on long non‐coding RNAs (lncRNAs), which are RNA molecules that do not code for proteins but play crucial roles in various biological processes.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study identified 17 lncRNAs altered by the influenza virus, with a focus on SNHG15's role in enhancing influenza virus infection.
analysis.methods: Knockdown of SNHG15 using CRISPR interference and RNA interference was performed, along with RNA pull‐down and mass spectrometry to identify Rab‐like protein 2A (RABL2A) as an interacting partner of SNHG15.
analysis.main_results: Knockdown of SNHG15 reduced influenza virus infection, while overexpression increased virus replication. miR‐153‐3p, a competitive endogenous RNA for SNHG15, acts as an anti‐influenza microRNA, and its overexpression negated SNHG15's proviral activity. Both SNHG15 and RABL2A facilitated influenza virus internalization.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that SNHG15 enhances influenza A virus infection through its interactions with miR‐153 and RABL2A, providing novel insights into the molecular mechanisms of influenza virus infection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings may inform the development of new therapeutic strategies targeting lncRNAs or their interacting partners to combat influenza virus infection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on in vitro experiments, and the evidence strength is moderate due to the lack of in vivo validation and clinical data.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the role of long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) in influenza virus infection, identifying SNHG15 as a key enhancer. The researchers found that SNHG15 promotes influenza virus infection by interacting with miR-153 and RABL2A. Knockdown of SNHG15 reduced infection, while overexpression increased replication. miR-153-3p counteracted SNHG15's proviral activity, and both SNHG15 and RABL2A facilitated viral internalization. These findings provide novel insights into the molecular mechanisms of influenza infection and may inform future therapeutic strategies targeting lncRNAs.

title: Assessment of Timing for Influenza Vaccination among Older Adults in Japan: The VENUS Study.

analysis.research_question_and_background: In Japan, seasonal influenza vaccination is recommended for older adults between October and mid-December; however, the optimal vaccination timing remains unclear owing to waning immunity and variable epidemic patterns. In this study, we aimed to assess the effectiveness of different vaccination strategies in reducing influenza-related outcomes in older adults.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Using data from the VENUS Study, we conducted a target trial emulation including adults aged ≥65 years across four influenza seasons (2016/2017, 2017/2018, 2018/2019, and 2019/2020). Outcomes included influenza, influenza-related hospitalization, and all-cause mortality.
analysis.methods: We applied a cloning, censoring, and weighting approach. Each individual was cloned and assigned to one of seven vaccination strategies at the start of October: no vaccination, vaccination during October, October-November, October-December, November, November-December, or December. Risk ratios (RRs) and risk differences (RDs), relative to no vaccination, were estimated at the end of March for each season based on standardized cumulative incidence.
analysis.main_results: Annual cohorts included 131,178-138,438 individuals (median age: 76-78 years; male sex: 40.1-41.0%). The influenza incidences and RRs varied by season. Delayed vaccination was associated with the lowest influenza incidence in 2017/2018 and 2018/2019, but not in the other seasons. Influenza-related hospitalizations showed seasonal trends similar to those of influenza. In contrast, early vaccination strategies generally led to reduced all-cause mortality across all seasons. The RRs were 0.80-0.93, 0.80-0.95, 0.82-1.00, and 0.81-0.96 in the 2016/2017, 2017/2018, 2018/2019, and 2019/2020 seasons, respectively. The RDs were larger for mortality than for the influenza-related outcomes.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The effectiveness of each timing strategy varied depending on the outcome and season. Although delayed vaccination was associated with a lower influenza incidence in some seasons, early vaccination generally reduced all-cause mortality.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that vaccination timing should be tailored to the season and outcome, with early vaccination potentially reducing mortality despite variable effects on influenza incidence. This could inform public health recommendations for optimizing influenza vaccination strategies in older adults.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study used target trial emulation, which may introduce limitations inherent to observational data. However, the large sample size and consistent results across multiple seasons provide moderate confidence in the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study assessed the optimal timing for influenza vaccination in older adults in Japan using data from the VENUS Study across four seasons. Researchers evaluated seven vaccination strategies, including no vaccination, and measured outcomes such as influenza incidence, hospitalization, and mortality. Results showed that delayed vaccination reduced influenza incidence in some seasons, but early vaccination consistently lowered all-cause mortality across all seasons. The effectiveness varied by season and outcome, with risk ratios for mortality ranging from 0.80 to 1.00. The findings suggest that vaccination timing should be tailored to the season and outcome, with early vaccination potentially offering mortality benefits despite variable effects on influenza incidence.

The findings highlight the importance of such training for pandemic preparedness, though periodic refresher courses may be needed to maintain current knowledge.

title: Parameterization of the PA Endonuclease Bimetallic Center Reveals the Dynamics of Clinically Relevant Mutations.

analysis.study_design_and_population: This study systematically benchmarked metal-parametrization strategies for molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the wild-type PA N-terminal endonuclease domain (PAN) in both apo and drug-bound states.
analysis.methods: The researchers evaluated nonbonded, bonded, and hybrid models for parametrization and used the identified reliable schemes to perform MD simulations of five clinically relevant mutants (I38T/F/M, A36V, and E23K).
analysis.main_results: The MD simulations revealed how each clinically relevant mutation reshapes the conformational landscape to modulate drug-binding modes in the PAN active site.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret their findings as providing a path toward modeling complex sites in metalloenzymes and a mechanistic foundation for vulnerabilities in PAN to guide the optimization of next-generation inhibitors.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results offer a mechanistic foundation for targeting PAN vulnerabilities, which can inform the structure-based design of improved antiviral therapies against influenza A virus.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on computational modeling, which may not fully capture in vivo biological complexities, but the systematic benchmarking and direct simulation of clinically relevant mutations provide high confidence in the mechanistic insights.

analysis.summary_en: This study addresses the challenge of resistance mutations to the antiviral baloxavir marboxil (BXM) in influenza A virus by systematically benchmarking metal-parametrization strategies for molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the PA N-terminal endonuclease domain (PAN). The researchers evaluated nonbonded, bonded, and hybrid models, then applied reliable schemes to simulate five clinically relevant mutants (I38T/F/M, A36V, and E23K). The results revealed how each mutation reshapes the conformational landscape to modulate drug-binding modes, providing a mechanistic foundation for targeting PAN vulnerabilities. This work offers a path for modeling complex metalloenzyme sites and guides the structure-based optimization of next-generation influenza inhibitors.

title: Near real-time data on the human neutralizing antibody landscape to influenza virus as of early 2026 to inform vaccine-strain selection

analysis.methods: To characterize the antigenic properties of current seasonal influenza A strains, the researchers conducted neutralization assays using a library of hemagglutinins reflecting the circulating diversity of strains in late 2025 to early 2026.

analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform vaccine-strain selection for the 2026-2027 Northern Hemisphere vaccine and provide insights into the evolution of influenza immunity.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to data collected in late 2025, and the evidence is based on a single dataset from that time period, which may affect the generalizability of the results.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Infectious Disease Surveillance: Applications, Challenges, and Future Perspectives

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the critical role of infectious disease surveillance in global public health systems and explores how artificial intelligence can overcome limitations of traditional surveillance methods.

title: Influenza Associated Encephalopathy, Encephalitis, and Acute Necrotizing Encephalitis in Adults: A Scoping Review of 83 Cases

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza-associated encephalopathy, encephalitis, and acute necrotizing encephalopathy are rare but potentially life-threatening neurological complications of influenza, and adult cases remain poorly characterized due to limited literature.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A PRISMA-guided scoping review of the MEDLINE database was conducted through 31 May 2026, analyzing 83 adult cases reported between 1958 and 2026.
analysis.methods: Published adult cases of influenza-associated encephalopathy, encephalitis, and acute necrotizing encephalopathy were identified and analyzed for demographic characteristics, clinical presentation, neuroimaging findings, treatment, and outcomes.
analysis.main_results: Eighty-three adult cases were included, with a mean age of 45.6 ± 17.8 years, 57.8% male, and two-thirds without underlying comorbidities; neurological symptoms developed a mean of 4.6 days after influenza onset, with influenza A accounting for 80.7% of infections.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that these complications are rare in adults but associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, and this review represents the largest adult cohort reported to date, providing important insights into the clinical spectrum, neurodiagnostic findings, and outcomes.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This review highlights significant gaps in knowledge and the need for collaborative multicenter studies to improve the diagnosis, treatment, and outcome of these severe complications of influenza infection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate due to the scoping review design, which relies on case reports and small case series, limiting generalizability and introducing potential biases.

analysis.summary_en: This scoping review analyzed 83 adult cases of influenza-associated encephalopathy, encephalitis, and acute necrotizing encephalopathy reported between 1958 and 2026. The mean age was 45.6 years, with 57.8% male and two-thirds without comorbidities. Neurological symptoms appeared 4.6 days post-influenza onset, with influenza A accounting for 80.7% of cases. Common manifestations included fever (91.6%), altered mental status (86.7%), and seizures (36.1%). Encephalitis was the predominant presentation (44.5%), followed by encephalopathy (31.3%) and ANE (24.1%). MRI frequently showed cerebral hemispheric lesions (53.0%) and bilateral thalamic involvement (36.4%), with EEG abnormalities in 69.6% of patients. Overall mortality was 22.9%, highest in ANE (45.0%), and 28.9% of survivors had persistent neurological sequelae. This review represents the largest adult cohort to date, highlighting substantial morbidity and mortality and the need for collaborative studies to improve diagnosis and treatment.

title: Characterization of Influenza A HA and NA Subtypes Using Protein Sequences

title: Viral Etiology of Acute Bronchiolitis in Hospitalized Infants in Casablanca, Morocco: A Prospective Autumn–Winter 2025–2026 Series and Implications for Prevention

analysis.research_question_and_background: Acute bronchiolitis is the leading cause of infant hospitalization worldwide, with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) historically predominating. Prospective virological data for the 2025–2026 epidemic season in Morocco were lacking.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A prospective observational cohort study was conducted at the Department of Pediatric Infectious Diseases and Clinical Immunology, Casablanca Mother-Child Hospital, from August 2025 through March 2026. Consecutive infants aged 1–24 months hospitalized with acute viral bronchiolitis underwent nasopharyngeal sampling and multiplex rapid antigen testing for RSV, influenza A, influenza B, and SARS-CoV-2.
analysis.methods: A total of 131 infants were enrolled (median age 4.8 months; male-to-female ratio 0.84:1). At least one virus was identified in 63 patients (48.1%; 95% CI 39.1–57.3%).
analysis.main_results: RSV predominated: 49 sole infections and 2 co-infections with influenza A, totaling 51 positives (80.9% of virus-positive cases; 38.9% of the cohort). Influenza A totaled 8 cases (12.7%), including the 2 co-infections; influenza B accounted for 2 further cases (3.2%). SARS-CoV-2 was not detected.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study provides updated virological data on acute bronchiolitis in Moroccan infants, confirming RSV as the predominant pathogen while also identifying influenza A and B as significant contributors. The findings highlight the need for targeted preventive measures in this population.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: All detected pathogens have licensed preventive options, supporting the introduction of nirsevimab, maternal RSV vaccination, and seasonal influenza vaccination as public health priorities in Morocco. This data can inform local vaccination strategies and surveillance programs.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited to a single center and used rapid antigen testing, which may have reduced sensitivity for some viruses. Despite these limitations, the prospective design and comprehensive testing provide moderate evidence for the local epidemiology of bronchiolitis viruses.

analysis.summary_en: This prospective observational study conducted in Casablanca, Morocco from August 2025 to March 2026 investigated the viral etiology of acute bronchiolitis in hospitalized infants aged 1-24 months. Among 131 enrolled infants, 63 (48.1%) tested positive for at least one virus, with RSV predominating at 51 cases (38.9% of cohort, 80.9% of positives). Influenza A was detected in 8 cases (12.7%) and influenza B in 2 cases (3.2%), while SARS-CoV-2 was not found. The epidemic peaked in January 2026. The authors recommend implementing preventive measures including nirsevimab, maternal RSV vaccination, and seasonal influenza vaccination as public health priorities in Morocco.

title: Development and Evaluation of a Multiplex Lateral Flow Immunoassay for Multiple Respiratory Virus Detection

analysis.research_question_and_background: Simultaneous detection of influenza A virus (IAV), influenza B virus (IBV), and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is essential for rapid differential diagnosis in febrile patients, particularly in the context of co-circulating respiratory viruses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study aimed to develop a multicolor latex-based immunochromatographic strip as a rapid, sensitive, and reliable tool for analyte detection. Methods: In this study, a multicolor latex microsphere-based immunochromatographic assay was developed for the rapid and simultaneous detection of SARS-CoV-2, IAV, and IBV antigens.
analysis.methods: The analytical and clinical performance of the assay were systematically evaluated.
analysis.main_results: The assay enabled detection within 15 minutes, with a limit of detection (LOD) of 102 TCID50/mL for all three viruses. Clinical evaluation showed a sensitivity of 97.73% (215/220) and specificity of 100% (200/200) for SARS-CoV-2 detection, with an overall concordance rate of 98.81% (415/420) and a Kappa value of 0.9762 (p < 0.05), indicating excellent agreement with reference methods.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: This multicolor latex-based immunochromatographic strip exhibits rapid, sensitive, and reliable performance for analyte detection without requiring specialized training.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: It shows strong potential for home self-testing and early screening in settings where SARS-CoV-2 and influenza co-circulate.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report limitations related to the study design or sample size.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to develop a multicolor latex-based immunochromatographic strip for the rapid and simultaneous detection of SARS-CoV-2, influenza A virus (IAV), and influenza B virus (IBV). The assay was evaluated for analytical and clinical performance, demonstrating detection within 15 minutes with a limit of detection of 102 TCID50/mL for all three viruses. Clinical results showed high sensitivity (97.73%) and specificity (100%) for SARS-CoV-2, with an overall concordance rate of 98.81% and a Kappa value of 0.9762, indicating strong agreement with reference methods. The assay is reliable, does not require specialized training, and has potential for home self-testing and early screening in co-circulating virus settings. The evidence is limited to abstract-only data, and no specific limitations are reported.

title: Quantum-Classical Reservoir Computing to Predict Influenza H3N2 Antigenic Distance

analysis.research_question_and_background: Accurate prediction of antigenic distance between influenza A/H3N2 strains is essential for timely vaccine strain selection, yet traditional hemagglutination inhibition (HI) assays are labour-intensive and limited in throughput.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We present FluQRC, a hybrid Quantum-Classical Reservoir Computing framework for sequence-based antigenic distance prediction.
analysis.methods: On two datasets spanning 1963-2002 (271 strains, 73,441 pairs) and 2003-2025 (888 strains, 788,544 pairs), FluQRC is competitive with four established baselines on the historical set and outperforms all of them on the larger, more challenging 2003-2025 set.
analysis.main_results: FluQRC attains MAE = 0.369, RMSE = 0.635, and R 2 = 0.900 on the 2003-2025 set, a 20.3% reduction in MAE and 14.3% reduction in RMSE over the strongest baseline, raising R 2 from 0.862 to 0.900.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These results demonstrate the scalability and effectiveness of FluQRC for large-scale antigenic distance prediction.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that FluQRC could improve the efficiency and accuracy of influenza vaccine strain selection by providing a faster, high-throughput alternative to traditional assays.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on abstract-only evidence, and while the results are promising, further validation with additional datasets and real-world applications is needed to confirm robustness.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces FluQRC, a hybrid Quantum-Classical Reservoir Computing framework for predicting antigenic distance between influenza A/H3N2 strains. Tested on two datasets (1963-2002 and 2003-2025), FluQRC outperformed established baselines on the larger dataset, achieving MAE = 0.369, RMSE = 0.635, and R2 = 0.900—a 20.3% reduction in MAE and 14.3% reduction in RMSE over the strongest baseline. The results demonstrate FluQRC's scalability and effectiveness for large-scale antigenic distance prediction, offering a potential high-throughput alternative to traditional labor-intensive assays like hemagglutination inhibition. While promising, further validation is needed to confirm robustness in real-world applications.
